evidence.title: Implementing an AI algorithm in the clinical setting: a case study for the accuracy paradox
evidence.outcome: Users misjudging AI accuracy because metrics not presented at local prevalence
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 100% and specificity 92% but false discovery rate 67% and PPV 33%, leading to perception of inaccuracy and removal of the tool.
evidence.quote: While the sensitivity of the algorithm at our institution was even higher than the manufacturer's reported values, the false discovery rate was 67%, leading to the perception that the algorithm was inaccurate.
evidence.sample_unit: patients undergoing CTA in the emergency department

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether presenting screening AI performance as expected true- and false-positive patient counts at intended-population prevalence, compared with standard care, changes how users judge the tool or act on its output. One emergency department study of 48 patients reported sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 92% alongside a positive predictive value of 33%, and the gap between these figures may have contributed to users' removal of the tool.

perspectives.view: No included study compares count-based presentation at local prevalence with relative metrics or any other format. The single available study is a descriptive, cross-sectional report of 48 patients, and it documents the hazard rather than testing the practice. Certainty that the practice improves interpretation cannot be rated, so it is classed as no direct evidence.

The emergency department study found a false discovery rate of 67%, meaning two of every three positive flags were wrong at that site's prevalence. Users who expected accuracy near the reported 92% specificity perceived the tool as unreliable. The study suggests that misreading metrics can cause abandonment as well as overtrust, but it does not show that counts would prevent either.

In a real deployment, clinicians discontinued a tool whose headline sensitivity and specificity did not match the positive predictive value they experienced. This observation suggests that performance summaries not matched to local prevalence may set expectations that the workflow then contradicts. Whether count-based displays would be read correctly at the point of care has not been studied.

FDA's draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions describes this format and gives a worked example of 0.8 false positives per true positive, compared with standard care and with a worst case of 4. The guidance is a draft and describes the approach rather than requiring it, and no cited study evaluates its effect.

The one deployment study ended with removal of the tool after users judged it inaccurate at a 33% positive predictive value. This suggests that a purchase and implementation effort may be lost when expected local performance is not set out before go-live. The cost and staff time needed to produce prevalence-specific counts for each site have not been measured.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that randomize clinicians or patients to count-based presentation at intended-population prevalence versus sensitivity and specificity alone, and that measure accuracy of interpretation, trust calibration, tool retention, and downstream testing. These studies should also examine how developers and deployers obtain reliable local prevalence estimates and how often the counts must be updated as prevalence shifts.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the single hazard study of 48 emergency department patients in the United States did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or literacy characteristics. Prevalence often differs in safety-net populations, so counts calculated for one population may misstate expected false positives in another. The effect of count-based formats on low-literacy or limited English proficiency users is unknown.
